title: In situ reversal of established keloids and pathological cutaneous scars

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a treatment that transforms an established keloid or hypertrophic scar into durable normal dermis while leaving the tissue in place. It would remodel the abnormal extracellular matrix and normalize the fibroblast states that produce and maintain it. Success would mean restoration of dermal architecture and mechanical behavior, beyond a reduction in scar height or volume. This is a target capability, not an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

Conceptual distinction: preventing a new wound from becoming fibrotic, removing an existing scar, preventing recurrence after removal, and reversing an existing scar are different outcomes. Excision removes the lesion and creates a new wound; it does not itself demonstrate conversion of the original scar into normal tissue. The defining advance here is restoration within the established lesion, without requiring its excision.

significance.text: Pathological scars can impair function, alter appearance, and cause psychological distress. Yang, Liu, and Cheng’s review connects scar formation to fibroblast activity, extracellular-matrix organization, and mechanical signaling. These features explain why the target extends beyond cosmetic flattening: a convincing reversal would restore the organization and physical behavior of tissue that has already become fibrotic.

Conditional significance: successful in situ restoration would establish that established cutaneous fibrosis can be reversed in the scar types and circumstances tested. Stable flattening, softening, and mechanical normalization would follow directly from the proposed endpoint. Improvements in movement, comfort, or quality of life would be important clinical outcomes to measure separately; tissue normalization alone would not quantify those benefits.

Limits and downstream possibilities: efficacy in keloids would not establish efficacy in hypertrophic scars, and neither result would automatically extend to systemic sclerosis. Application to another fibrotic disease would require evidence that the relevant cellular programs, matrix abnormalities, and treatment requirements are sufficiently shared. The therapeutic class would not determine whether an advance qualifies: an improved steroid-based treatment could qualify if it achieved durable in situ normalization, whereas a lower recurrence rate after excision and radiation would demonstrate a different capability.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is coordinated restoration of both the established scar matrix and the cellular behavior that sustains it. The reviewed biology identifies fibroblasts, matrix remodeling, and mechanotransduction as relevant, including discussion of YAP and Engrailed-1. Normal dermis has a basket-weave collagen organization, whereas the review describes post-traumatic collagen as more parallel. Reaching the proposed endpoint therefore requires more than suppressing new collagen production or reducing lesion size.

Engineering synthesis: a successful intervention would need to remodel existing abnormal matrix while preserving tissue integrity, bring fibroblast behavior toward a normal dermal state, and leave a stable tissue environment after treatment ends. These requirements make selective, coordinated remodeling central to the challenge. Matrix reduction without adequate rebuilding could fail the structural or mechanical endpoint, while temporary suppression of fibroblast activity could leave the underlying lesion capable of renewed fibrosis.

Translational synthesis: mechanisms that redirect healing immediately after injury must be shown to work in an already established pathological scar. Concrete unresolved questions include which cellular states must change, how much mature matrix must be replaced, whether the remodeled tissue remains stable under local mechanical forces, and whether the same intervention works across different scar types and previously recurrent lesions. The supplied evidence does not identify a validated intervention that resolves this full set of requirements.

current_state.text: Yang, Liu, and Cheng’s October 2025 review reported that scar-free wound healing remained unavailable in clinical practice and surveyed fibroblast, matrix, and signaling mechanisms relevant to regenerative repair. This supports a dated account of a clinical regenerative gap. Its statement concerns wound healing; it is not a systematic assessment of every treatment for reversing established keloids or hypertrophic scars. The supplied material therefore does not establish that no human therapy achieves the proposed endpoint as of November 1, 2026.

The review’s YAP and Engrailed-1 discussions concern experimental wound repair and do not demonstrate in situ reversal of an established human keloid. The earlier description of these as mouse studies cannot be retained without qualification: the YAP subsection describes verteporfin-treated rat wounds followed after an operation, and the supplied evidence review identified mismatches between narrative attributions and listed references. In particular, the relevant YAP reference is a Horsley commentary, while the Engrailed-1 narrative points to a reference listed as a Leavitt Prrx1 study. These inconsistencies limit attribution of the specific animal results; they do not establish that the underlying results are false.

The research notes attribute to Cardenas and colleagues a review of major keloids that could not be closed primarily, published online December 26, 2024, in a 2025 journal volume. The notes report 51 recurrences among 244 patients, approximately 21%, and a 45–100% recurrence range drawn from earlier excision-alone series. They also attribute to that article a characterization of excision plus radiation as a mainstay. No article artifact was supplied for inspection in the validated review, so the population, treatment mix, follow-up, numerical results, and treatment characterization remain unverified here. The earlier statement that the excision-alone range had been inspected in the article text is not supported by the supplied evidence record.

The research notes also attribute an approximately 19% recurrence estimate after surgery plus one adjuvant to Ellis and colleagues, with an August 2020 publication date. The supplied PubMed artifact contains only a cookie-access message. It does not permit confirmation of article identity, study completeness, treatment details, or the estimate. This figure remains an unresolved report from the notes, not an established result in this record. Even a verified postoperative recurrence estimate would address control after removal, rather than reversal of the original lesion.

The supplied review assessed an untruncated text extraction of the Yang article, including its body, conclusions, and references; figure images were not supplied or inspected. That provides substantive textual support for its dated clinical statement and biological discussion, subject to the citation inconsistencies described above. No bounded freshness-search record was supplied, so this account cannot be treated as a comprehensive assessment of treatment availability through November 1, 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: treat established keloids in place, including lesions that have previously recurred, and show regression to soft, flat tissue without excision. Compare the resulting tissue with adjacent uninjured skin using collagen architecture, mechanical measurements, and histological and cellular assessments. The review’s discussion of normal collagen organization and scar mechanics supports the relevance of these endpoints, but the complete demonstration proposed here is not an established consensus standard.
completion_criteria.label: Established keloids, including recurrent lesions, soften and flatten without excision

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evidence of tissue restoration: show that matrix organization and fibroblast states approach those of normal dermis, alongside clinically meaningful mechanical recovery. Measurements should distinguish normalization from simple volume reduction, temporary suppression, or replacement by another abnormal tissue state. The intervention and assessment methods should be described sufficiently for independent groups to reproduce the result, with comparisons that support attributing restoration to treatment.
completion_criteria.label: Matrix and fibroblast states approach normal with mechanical recovery

completion_criteria.text: Proposed durability threshold: observe no recurrence in the evaluated lesions over three years after treatment, with the need for maintenance treatment explicitly reported. Three years is a proposed observation period, not a source-endorsed threshold or proof of permanent nonrecurrence. A convincing report would disclose the number of patients and lesions, follow-up completeness, recurrence definition, adverse effects, and uncertainty around the observed outcome.
completion_criteria.label: No recurrence over three years, with maintenance treatment reported

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: establish the result separately in hypertrophic scars before claiming the broader capability, and report performance across the lesion sizes, anatomical sites, prior treatments, and patient groups actually evaluated. Independent replication and broader clinical testing would establish demonstrated breadth, not universal efficacy. Low recurrence after excision plus radiation would remain outside the central criterion because the original scar was removed rather than restored in situ.
completion_criteria.label: Hypertrophic scar restoration demonstrated separately, with evaluated breadth reported

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: DER-01, “Clinical restoration of a complete human skin organ,” overlaps in the goal of restoring normal skin structure and function. DER-10 specifically concerns reversal within an established pathological scar; complete skin-organ restoration is a broader endpoint that may include structures beyond the dermis. Prevention of fibrosis during a fresh wound and reversal of an existing scar should remain distinct. Only DER-01’s title was supplied, so its precise routes and completion criteria cannot be inferred.

Roster-based synthesis: DER-09, “Durable regenerative closure of diabetic foot ulcers after ischemia and pressure are treated,” shares a concern with regenerative repair but begins with an open chronic wound. DER-10 begins with an established scar and asks whether its abnormal tissue can be normalized. Closing an ulcer and reversing fibrosis require separate demonstrations; neither endpoint establishes the other.

Roster-based synthesis: DER-03, “Antigen-selective erasure of pathogenic cutaneous immune memory,” targets persistent pathogenic immunity, whereas DER-10 targets established fibrotic matrix and fibroblast states. DER-07 concerns prevention of atopic dermatitis and the atopic march, and DER-08 concerns rebuilding a depleted melanocyte stem-cell reservoir. These entries address different biological deficits. A treatment’s effect on inflammation, disease prevention, or pigmentation would not by itself establish reversal of scar tissue.

Roster-based synthesis: DER-02 targets a one-time genomic cure of severe monogenic skin disease through epidermal stem cells, and DER-04 targets programmable delivery across intact stratum corneum. Delivery technology could become relevant if a scar-reversal treatment required macromolecules or gene editors, but successful delivery or correction of an epidermal mutation would not demonstrate dermal normalization. DER-05 and DER-06 address ultraviolet-related cancer prevention through DNA repair or resetting mutant epidermal fields; those endpoints remain distinct from reversal of cutaneous fibrosis.

change_log.change: Preserved DER-10’s ID, title, and central goal while defining restoration as coordinated matrix remodeling and fibroblast-state normalization.
change_log.reason: The concept remains coherent despite gaps in individual supporting assertions; the review supplies useful biological distinctions that sharpen its identity.

change_log.change: Replaced categorical claims of universal treatment absence with a dated clinical limitation and an explicit limit on present-day conclusions.
change_log.reason: The October 2025 review addresses scar-free wound healing and does not establish comprehensive treatment availability for established scars through November 1, 2026.

change_log.change: Reframed excision as lesion removal followed by a new wound, without asserting that it inevitably restarts the same pathological program.
change_log.reason: Removal and recurrence prevention differ from in situ reversal, but the deterministic account of recurrence was not established.

change_log.change: Retained the Cardenas and Ellis numerical reports with explicit attribution and access limitations.
change_log.reason: The user requested preservation of unresolved quantitative detail. No Cardenas artifact was supplied, and the Ellis artifact contained only a cookie-access message; neither limitation proves the reported results false.

change_log.change: Qualified the animal-study account and incorporated the rat-model description and citation mismatches.
change_log.reason: The supplied review does not securely support the earlier mouse-specific attribution or a claim of established human-keloid reversal.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed demonstration to include cellular measurements, independent reproducibility, scar-type-specific evidence, and practical reporting boundaries.
change_log.reason: Flattening alone does not establish the stated biological endpoint, and a keloid demonstration does not cover hypertrophic scars.

change_log.change: Clarified that three years without observed recurrence is a proposed durability endpoint.
change_log.reason: It is neither an established standard nor proof of permanent nonrecurrence.

change_log.change: Removed unverified demographic and lesion-behavior assertions from the significance argument and made systemic-sclerosis applications conditional.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence supports functional and psychological burden but does not verify the darker-skin burden, extension beyond injury boundaries, or generalization to another fibrotic disease.

change_log.change: Replaced blanket dismissal of existing treatment classes with an outcome-based distinction.
change_log.reason: An improved treatment could satisfy the concept if it achieved durable in situ normalization; its drug class alone does not determine the magnitude of the advance.

change_log.reason: The roster permits useful comparison, but full definitions and evidence records for those innovations were not supplied.

change_log.reason: They concern selection of the wider innovation list rather than evidence for DER-10.

unresolved_issues: Whether any human therapy had demonstrated durable in situ normalization of established keloids or hypertrophic scars by November 1, 2026 remains undetermined; the supplied freshness-search record is empty.
The Cardenas population, treatment mix, follow-up, 51/244 recurrence result, 45–100% excision-alone range, and mainstay characterization require inspectable article evidence.
The Ellis article identity, approximately 19% estimate, treatment definition, and follow-up remain unverified because the supplied artifact contains only a cookie-access message.
Primary studies are needed to resolve species, intervention, attribution, and outcome details in the Yang review’s YAP and Engrailed-1 discussions.
The extent to which keloids and hypertrophic scars share a therapeutically reversible program remains unresolved; success in one cannot establish the other.
The assays, acceptable degree of normalization, and practical sampling strategy for demonstrating restored fibroblast states, matrix architecture, and mechanics remain to be specified.
The three-year observation period has not been established as sufficient for clinical adoption or long-term recurrence assessment.
Application to systemic sclerosis remains a hypothesis requiring disease-specific evidence.

The review’s recommendation to remove the unverified recurrence figures entirely was not adopted: the figures were retained as explicitly unverified reports to preserve quantitative detail without presenting them as validated findings.

brief.title: Restoring established raised scars to normal skin
possible: People with keloids or hypertrophic scars, types of raised scar, could have the affected tissue restored without cutting it out. Treatment would turn an established scar into soft, flat tissue with the structure and physical behaviour of normal skin.
The change would last after treatment ends. It would rebuild the tissue already there, including its supporting material and the cells that keep producing scar tissue.
why: Pathological scars can restrict function, change appearance and cause psychological distress. Restoring their structure would address the tissue changes behind their stiffness and raised shape.
Success would establish that established scarring can be reversed in the kinds of scars treated. Movement, comfort and quality of life would also be important outcomes to measure.

sources.who: Wenhui Yang, Liu Liu and Xingjian Cheng
sources.showed: Their review describes how tissue-building cells, supporting material and mechanical forces contribute to scarring. It reports experimental work on healing wounds without scars.
sources.quote: Excessive and disorganized deposition of collagen and matrix leads to scarring.
sources.cited_for: Restoration requires changes to both scar structure and the cells that sustain it.
sources.not_established: The review does not demonstrate lasting restoration of an established human keloid.

sources.showed: This is a review of treatment for major keloids whose surgical wounds could not be closed directly.
sources.cited_for: It concerns treatment involving scar removal and subsequent recurrence.
sources.not_established: Outcomes after removal do not establish restoration of the original scar in place.

sources.showed: Their combined analysis compared keloid recurrence after surgery with different combinations of added treatments. Some combinations had lower recurrence.
sources.quote: The differences for surgery and intralesional triamcinolone (TAC) showed trends toward significance
sources.cited_for: Combining treatments can improve control of keloids after surgical removal.
sources.not_established: The analysis measured recurrence after removal, rather than conversion of an existing scar into normal tissue.

shown: Yang, Liu and Cheng describe experimental progress in directing wound healing away from scarring. Ellis and colleagues report control of keloid recurrence after surgery. Neither demonstrates lasting restoration of an established human scar while leaving it in place.
missing: Existing abnormal scar material must be rebuilt into normal tissue while preserving its strength and integrity.
Fibroblasts, the cells that produce scar material, must return towards normal behaviour alongside recovery of tissue mechanics.
Restored tissue must remain stable after treatment ends, including in scars that have previously returned.
Restoration must be demonstrated separately in keloids and hypertrophic scars.

milestones.label: Established and recurrent keloids become soft and flat without removal
milestones.explanation: Treated keloids, including previously recurrent lesions, would have to become soft and flat, with tissue compared against nearby uninjured skin. This would establish regression while leaving the original tissue in place.

milestones.label: Scar structure and cells approach normal as mechanics recover
milestones.explanation: Supporting material and fibroblast behaviour would have to approach normal alongside meaningful mechanical recovery, with reproducible measurements. This would distinguish restoration from shrinkage or temporary suppression.

milestones.label: Scars stay absent for three years, with maintenance reported
milestones.explanation: Treated lesions would have to remain free of recurrence for three years, with maintenance treatment and follow-up completeness reported. This would test durability over the proposed observation period.

milestones.label: Hypertrophic scars recover separately, with treatment breadth reported
milestones.explanation: Restoration would have to be demonstrated separately in hypertrophic scars, with results across the scar sizes, sites and patient groups tested. Independent replication would establish how broadly the treatment works.

uncertain: It remains unclear which cell behaviours must change and how much mature scar material must be replaced.
The acceptable degree of structural, cellular and mechanical recovery still needs defining.
The proposed three-year follow-up may not be sufficient to judge long-term recurrence.

page.title: In situ reversal of keloids and hypertrophic scars
page.definition: Treatment remodels an established keloid or hypertrophic scar in place into dermis—the connective tissue beneath the epidermis—with normal matrix architecture and mechanical properties. Restoration persists after treatment ends.

goal.need: Across 10 surgical studies of major keloids whose defects could not be closed directly, 51 of 244 patients had recurrence, approximately 21%. These results concern lesions removed surgically. The German S2k guideline describes goals such as 30–50% volume reduction or symptom reduction above 50% after 3–6 sessions or months; neither endpoint establishes restoration of the original dermis.

statements.body: German Dermatological Society and four participating medical societies
statements.quote: the main consideration is to alleviate the patient’s complaints.
statements.context: The S2k guideline makes treatment goals individual to the patient.

statements.quote: not only by reducing the volume of the scar but also alleviating associated symptoms such as pain and itch.
statements.context: The stated aims of SATELLITE, a study of topical SNT-6302 in established keloids.

statements.body: National Institute of General Medical Sciences
statements.quote: Scientists are studying regeneration for its potential uses in medicine, such as treating a variety of injuries and diseases.
statements.context: This is a general regenerative-medicine objective; the document does not set a scar-reversal endpoint.

completion.title: Established pathological scars regain normal dermal structure and mechanics for nine months without treatment.
completion.criterion: For each scar type, a controlled human study treats established lesions without excision. At treatment completion and through at least nine months without further scar treatment, lesions have separate POSAS 2.0 patient and observer sums of 6, collagen architecture and fibroblast profiles within prespecified healthy-dermis reference intervals, and mechanical properties within matched healthy-skin reference intervals. A concurrent control establishes that restoration is attributable to treatment.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; proposed composite test using POSAS normal-skin anchors and SATELLITE's nine-month post-treatment follow-up schedule.
completion.basis: Searched FDA guidance and regulations, the German S2k scar guideline, POSAS instructions and scar-trial protocols for an established-scar reversal criterion; none supplied a combined structural, mechanical and treatment-free durability test. This Atlas test combines clinical normality with dermal restoration. Nine months comes from SATELLITE's follow-up schedule and is not a consensus definition of cure.

milestones.title: A scar-reversal drug has nonclinical evidence supporting reasonably safe human dosing.
milestones.criterion: Animal or in vitro pharmacology and toxicology support reasonably safe exposure in the proposed human investigation under 21 CFR 312.23(a)(8). Required studies depend on the investigation's nature and duration; there is no universal numerical safety margin. Supporting laboratory evidence includes a 2022 PXS-6302 experiment involving 12 porcine burn injuries across treatment and control groups, with no significant tensile-strength difference. Treatment began at re-epithelialisation; this experiment did not establish reversal of mature pathological scars.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 312.23(a)(8). This gate describes the medicinal development route for either scar type.
milestones.threshold_quote: the sponsor has concluded that it is reasonably safe to conduct the proposed clinical investigations.

milestones.title: People with an established pathological scar receive an in situ treatment in a phase 1 study.
milestones.criterion: Human administration begins with monitoring of pharmacological effects and adverse effects. For keloids, Syntara reported on 1 October 2026 that six SATELLITE participants completed 12 weeks of topical SNT-6302; eight discontinued because of local skin reactions. For hypertrophic sternotomy scars, SNT-9465 reached phase 1b administration, but recruitment was paused on 10 November 2026 after reports of mild to moderate skin irritation. These company results are not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 312.21(a)(1), defines the initial human-exposure stage. The cited Australian studies illustrate this stage in the two scar types.
milestones.threshold_quote: Phase 1 includes the initial introduction of an investigational new drug into humans.

milestones.title: An established pathological scar loses at least 50% of its height by week 12.
milestones.criterion: Use the height-response branch of NCT04812626's published efficacy definition: at least 50% reduction from baseline at 12 weeks after six intralesional injections, two weeks apart, of triamcinolone acetonide 20 mg/mL alone or with 5-fluorouracil 25 mg/mL. Participants were older than 15 years with scars at least 1 cm long. Published on 24 August 2024: 66 patients enrolled and 59 completed; 30/30 combination recipients and 21/29 steroid recipients completing follow-up met the height threshold. Results pooled scar types and did not assess recurrence.
milestones.set_by: B.P. Koirala Institute of Health Sciences investigators, published efficacy definition for registered trial NCT04812626; a trial-specific threshold covering both scar types.
milestones.threshold_quote: Efficacy was considered as a 50% or more reduction in the initial height

milestones.title: A treated pathological scar scores 6 on each POSAS 2.0 patient and observer scale.
milestones.criterion: Every item on each six-item Patient and Observer Scar Assessment Scale receives its normal-skin score of 1, giving two separate sums of 6 on scales ranging from 6 to 60. Assessment includes direct examination and palpation. This establishes clinical scar-quality normality before structural and durability confirmation. In NCT04812626, the 30 combination-treatment completers had mean observer and patient sums of 16.10 and 10.80 at week 12; these pooled summaries do not establish paired normal-skin scores for either scar type.
milestones.set_by: POSAS developers, User instructions POSAS 2.0, define the normal-skin anchor and separate patient and observer sums.
milestones.threshold_quote: The lowest score is ‘1’, which corresponds to the situation of normal skin (i.e. normal pigmentation, no itching).

not_found: No external criterion combining in situ dermal restoration, mechanical normalisation and treatment-free durability was located.
No accepted equivalence margins for restored collagen architecture, fibroblast profiles or scar mechanics were located.
No controlled human demonstration satisfying the proposed composite completion test was located.
ClinicalTrials.gov did not expose readable outcome text for NCT04812626; its efficacy threshold is documented here through the trial publication.
The supplied Yang review and Ellis PubMed record did not yield readable article text when opened.

results.finding: PXS-6302: 12 porcine burn injuries across treated and control groups; no significant tensile-strength difference.
results.detail: Treatment began at re-epithelialisation. This provides relevant nonclinical safety evidence, but the paper does not establish that the pharmacology and toxicology package supports reasonably safe exposure for a proposed human investigation.

results.finding: In a phase 1 keloid pilot, 4 patients received intralesional SVF; 0 reported adverse events.
results.detail: Patients were followed for three months, with scar assessments and adverse-event monitoring. The abstract calls the trial phase II, but the title and methods describe it as phase one.
results.quote: Among the SVF group, there were no reported adverse events in the entire follow-up period.

results.finding: Six patients with established keloids received calcium electroporation in a phase I study; 3 experienced transient ulceration.
results.detail: Researchers monitored scar response and adverse effects. One additional treated patient was excluded after biopsy showed a non-keloid scar.

results.finding: Six participants with keloid scars completed 12 weeks of topical SNT-6302 treatment.
results.detail: Eight participants discontinued treatment because of local skin reactions. The findings are preliminary and were reported by the company.
results.quote:

results.finding: In a 20-participant phase 1b hypertrophic sternotomy scar study, 60% had commenced SNT-9465 treatment.
results.detail: Participants had scars 6–24 months old and received active treatment and placebo on separate scar regions. The source describes planned scar assessments but does not state that adverse effects were monitored.
results.quote: Syntara Limited (ASX:SNT), a clinical-stage drug development company, is pleased to announce that recruitment in the Phase 1b study of its next-generation topical pan-lysyl oxidase (pan-LOX) inhibitor SNT-9465 in hypertrophic scars is progressing well, with 60% of participants now having commenced treatment.

results.finding: Among 59 completers with keloids or hypertrophic scars, 51/59 achieved at least 50% scar-height reduction by week 12.
results.detail: Results were pooled across scar types. After six injections two weeks apart, 30/30 combination recipients and 21/29 triamcinolone-only recipients met the threshold. Recurrence was not assessed.
results.quote: Similarly, in week 12, 50% or more reduction in the height was found significantly more in the TAC + 5‐FU group than in TAC alone group in both the ITT (96.9% vs. 67.7%) and PP population (100% vs. 72.4%)
